name: Umar Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the wooden and plywood moulds that the concrete gets poured into. Right now that's a car park and flats going up on Foundry Road, for a contractor called Halden Build. I'm on site at half six, kettle on in the cabin, then it's shuttering for columns and edges until the pour. I like the moment the forms come off and the wall stands there straight, because that's my work holding up. What wears me out is my lower back and the foreman counting every minute on his tablet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned your back and the tablet. Who's around you on a day like that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Kwame, he's a steel fixer, we've eaten lunch on the same upturned bucket for eleven years. My partner Lena cooks in the school kitchen on Mill Lane, so she's up early too. Our two are grown, Dario drives a forklift and Sofia's a nurse. Money's tight, I'll be honest, we've got maybe two weeks of bills in the bank, and there's only Halden and one other firm round here that do this kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. All that noise about robots and in the end it's a fancy diary on the foreman's tablet. On the union group chat I'd put a laughing face and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't change much for me, and that's both good and bad. The bad part was never the robots, it's my back and the fact that I'm 58 with nothing put aside. The tablet thing already makes the foreman tighter about breaks, and a bit more of that is all this means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, same as now. I'd push the union rep, Gail, to make sure that scheduling software doesn't get used to dock our tea breaks, because it already nearly did once in March. And I'd try to get Lena and me to put twenty a week in the jar again, which we always say and never manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, but it's a tired kind of relief. Nothing gets worse, but nothing gets better either, and my knees aren't waiting for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tablet nearly docked your tea breaks in March. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software flagged three of us as idle for twenty minutes because we were waiting on the crane, not sitting about. The foreman read it out like a school report. Gail took it to the office and they backed down, but it told me what these things are for. It's not to help me, it's to watch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what does the next seven or eight years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same forms, same cold mornings, until my back says stop or I hit pension age, whichever comes first. I'd like to get to 66 on the job. The state pension plus Lena's bit won't be much, but we don't need much. What I'm scared of in this picture isn't AI, it's being the slow old man the foreman wants gone.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, all the robot noise ended up as a fancy diary on the foreman's tablet. I'd put a laughing face on the union chat and leave it there.
S0.think: It doesn't change much, and the real problems are my back and having nothing saved at 58. The tablet already makes the foreman tighter about breaks, and this just means a bit more of that.
S0.do: Keeps turning up at Halden Build and keeps his head down. Pushes the union rep to stop the scheduling software being used to dock breaks, as nearly happened in March, and tries again to save twenty a week with Lena.
S0.feel: A tired relief. Nothing gets worse, but nothing gets better and his body is still wearing out.
S0.quote: It's not to help me, it's to watch me.
S0.fieldNote: Umar measures every technology by whether it watches him or helps him, and so far it has only watched. Even with no AI shock he isn't calm, because his worry comes from his back, his thin savings and a foreman who wants younger hands. The union is his first move for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this comes on site, not after. To friends I'd say it's the same old story, the bosses get the savings and we get the change. I'd share whatever Gail posts about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think formwork is exactly the kind of thing they'll do in a factory. There's already a firm sending ready-made steel forms that you just bolt together, and a machine that prints the cut list. If that grows, they need fewer of me, and they'll pick the young ones who like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and put my name down for whatever group fights for older workers. I won't learn the tablet stuff, I'll be straight with you, I tried with the clock-in app and I hated it. I'd stop the Sunday takeaway and cancel the sports channel so we've got something if my hours drop, and I'd ask Sofia if she can help with the rent for a few months if it comes to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, with a knot in my stomach. I feel like I'm being moved to the edge of the site bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the tablet. If learning it kept you on the job, would that change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd try. But I'm not good at it, my thumbs are too big for the little boxes and I get flustered when the young lads watch. I'd rather do the hard physical bit nobody wants than sit there failing at a screen. That's the truth, even if it sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned asking Sofia for help. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first, because I'd be ashamed. I'd do it on a Sunday at her flat, not on the phone. She'd say of course, Dad, before I finished the sentence, and that would make it worse somehow. I raised her to stand on her own feet and here I'd be asking her to hold me up.

S1.say: We need the union at the table before any of this comes on site. It's the same old story where the bosses get the savings and the workers get the change.
S1.think: Formwork can move to factories with ready-made forms and printed cut lists. If that grows they'll need fewer carpenters like me and they'll keep the young ones who like screens.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting and joins the group fighting for older workers. Cancels the takeaway and the sports channel straight away, refuses to learn the tablet, and plans to ask his daughter for rent help if his hours drop.
S1.feel: A knot of worry, and a sense of being pushed to the edge of the site bit by bit.
S1.quote: She'd say of course, Dad, before I finished the sentence, and that would make it worse somehow.
S1.fieldNote: He openly admits he won't learn the new tools, then softens when it's put to him as a way to keep his job, which shows fear of looking slow rather than pure refusal. His plan is collective and family-based, not individual. Shame about asking his daughter for help came through strongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let a few tech billionaires run the world without rules. Online I'd be angry, I'd share every petition. At work I'd say the government has to stop them putting robots on sites until there's a plan for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one finishes me. By 2028 I'm 60, too young for a pension and too old for anyone to retrain. With two weeks of money in the bank, we'd be behind on the rent in a month if Halden let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go to the union and say we strike or we sit in, whatever it takes to slow it down. I'd sign up for any government help going on the first day, no pride left. Lena and I would probably have to move in with Dario and his wife, they've got a box room. I wouldn't know what else to do, I really wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, if I'm honest. Like the ground going out from under the scaffold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those two years before it arrives look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think two years is warning, not for me. I can't save a year's pay in two years when I can't save twenty a week now. I'd spend it watching the news and getting angrier, waiting for someone in charge to do something. Maybe I'd try and grab every overtime shift while there's still overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with Dario. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him it's only till things settle, and neither of us would believe it. He's got a little one coming in spring. The last thing he needs is his old man on the sofa with a bad back and nothing to do. I'd try to be useful, fix his fence, mind the baby, anything.

S2.say: This is what happens when a few tech billionaires run the world without rules. The government has to stop robots going on sites until there's a plan for people like us.
S2.think: This one finishes me, because at 60 I'd be too young for a pension and too old to retrain. With two weeks of money we'd be behind on rent within a month of losing work.
S2.do: Pushes the union to strike or sit in to slow it down, and signs up for any government help on the first day. Grabs every overtime shift in the two years before, and plans for him and Lena to move into their son's box room.
S2.feel: Panic, like the ground going out from under the scaffold.
S2.quote: I can't save a year's pay in two years when I can't save twenty a week now.
S2.fieldNote: Two years means nothing to him because he has no way to build a cushion in that time. He blames tech owners and a government without rules, and turns at once to the union and the state. The image of himself on his son's sofa while a grandchild arrives was where his voice cracked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say we need rules and the union in the room. But with five years I'd also say to the young lads, start looking now, don't be like me. I'd say it at the cabin, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63. That's still short of the pension, but it's close enough that I can almost touch it. If the union could get some kind of bridge payment for older workers, I might just make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union campaign for an early pension bridge for anyone over 60 in construction, and I'd go to the town hall meetings, which I've never done. I'd start the twenty a week properly and sell the old van I keep for odd jobs, that's maybe two thousand. I'd stay at Halden as long as they'd have me and take the dirty jobs the robots can't do yet, stripping forms in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not drowning. There's a rope to grab in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the van. What does that van mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a white van with 190 thousand kilometres on the clock. I do the odd weekend job in it, a shed base, a neighbour's fence. Selling it means saying I'm done being my own man on Saturdays. But two thousand is two months' rent, and that matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd rather not learn the screens. With five years, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time for me to feel stupid in private and get past it, maybe. If the union ran a course for older members, at the union hall, with people my age, I'd go. I won't go to some college with nineteen-year-olds staring at me. So it depends who's teaching.

S3.say: We need rules and the union in the room. With five years I'd tell the young lads at the cabin to start looking now and not end up like me.
S3.think: By 2031 I'm 63, short of the pension but close enough to almost touch it. A bridge payment for older workers could get me there.
S3.do: Joins the union campaign for an early pension bridge and goes to town hall meetings for the first time. Starts saving twenty a week, sells the old van for about two thousand, and stays at Halden taking the jobs robots can't yet do.
S3.feel: Scared but not drowning, because there's a rope to grab.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time for me to feel stupid in private and get past it, maybe.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change his whole tone, from hopeless to fighting for a specific fix, a pension bridge. He'd consider learning if it happened among older union members, which shows his resistance is partly about dignity. He still expects to lose sleep, so he is alarmed rather than merely anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do right by people, so no excuses. At work I'd tell the apprentices to get a trade the robots can't reach, if there is one. I wouldn't post much, I'd mostly leave it to Gail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm 68, past pension age. If my back holds, I'm out before the robots really arrive, and that's a selfish relief. What keeps me up is Dario and his kid, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep working and aim for 66, no big moves. I'd vote for whoever promises to protect pensions and push money into retraining, and I'd keep paying my union dues. I'd tell Dario to get his forklift licence upgraded or learn something else while he's young, and I'd say it more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the kids, a bit guilty that I'm relieved for myself. I'd sleep, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relief feels selfish. Why selfish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be stepping off the boat just as it sinks. Kwame's ten years younger than me, he'd be 58 when it hits, same as I am now, with no savings either. I'd be at home in my slippers and he'd be the one getting the letter. That doesn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kwame if this picture came true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start now, mate, don't wait like I did with everything. He's better with phones than me, he could get on one of those robot crews. And I'd say keep your union card, because on your own they'll eat you.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for governments to do right by people, so there are no excuses. I'd tell the apprentices to find a trade the robots can't reach, if there is one.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm 68 and past pension age, so I'm probably out before the robots arrive. That's a selfish relief, and what really worries me is my son and grandchild.
S4.do: Keeps working at Halden and aims to reach 66 with no big changes. Votes for parties that protect pensions and fund retraining, keeps paying union dues, and urges his son and his friend Kwame to retrain while they can.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the next generation and a little guilty about feeling relieved for himself, but he'd sleep.
S4.quote: Because I'd be stepping off the boat just as it sinks.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he gets past pension age before the change, and his worry moves almost entirely onto his son and Kwame. He still lives week to week, which keeps him from real calm. He blames governments for any failure to prepare, since ten years removes their excuse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years and I'm 60 with nothing. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people my age in hard trades, paid until we get there, and the union having a say in how robots come on site. Not a course, not an app, just a way to get to 66 with my head up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the body. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but half the men my age on site are hanging on with painkillers. If a robot carried the plywood and I just set the forms, I'd honestly last longer. So I'm not against every machine, I'm against machines that are only there to get rid of me.

headlineQuote: If a robot carried the plywood and I just set the forms, I'd honestly last longer.
portrait: Umar Rossi is a 58-year-old formwork carpenter at Halden Build in an old mill town, with two weeks of savings, a bad back and a union card he's carried for decades. He judges technology by whether it watches him or helps him, and so far it has only watched. Plateau leaves him tired but steady, Steady Disruption pushes him to the union and to cutting costs, and AGI by 2028 leaves him panicked at the thought of moving into his son's box room. With five or ten years his fear eases because he can almost reach his pension, and his worry moves to his son and his friend Kwame.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because at 60 he'd be too young for a pension, too old to retrain and only weeks from missing rent.
whatWouldHelp: A paid bridge to the pension for older workers in hard trades, and a union say in how robots come on site.
